label: Timeline
notes: Open the timeline as a memory map for the course. The appendix is not about dates alone; it connects elastic curves, surface theory, topology, variational calculus, and Willmore geometry into one navigable storyline. Point out that the timeline is useful only when students use it to recover why a concept appeared.

label: The Timeline Has Three Lanes
notes: Use the lane diagram to prevent a flat chronology. One lane carries curve mechanics, one carries surface geometry, and one carries topology and invariance. The value is seeing when an idea moves lanes. Ask the room to classify each recent chapter by lane before naming the theorem.

label: Elastic Curves Become A Prototype
notes: Remind learners that elastic curves are the first complete variational laboratory. Curvature has a visible meaning, an energy, an Euler-Lagrange equation, and concrete reconstruction checks. This prototype later reappears whenever a surface problem is reduced to a one-dimensional curvature signal.

label: Surface Geometry Adds Area And Curvature
notes: Surfaces add two-dimensional bookkeeping. The metric supplies area, the shape operator supplies principal curvatures, and Gauss-Bonnet turns total Gaussian curvature into topology. This is the hinge where local differential data starts carrying global topological meaning.

label: Topology Explains What Cannot Change
notes: This slide should feel like a lock on deformation. Genus, orientation, and Euler characteristic are not numerical decorations; they decide which curvature integrals can change under smooth motion. When a family deforms smoothly, these quantities tell students what should stay fixed in the notebook checks.

label: Willmore Geometry Recombines The Threads
notes: Willmore geometry is the reunion point. It uses curvature energy like elastic curves, surface area and mean curvature like surface theory, topology through Gauss-Bonnet, and conformal invariance as a new organizing principle. The slide should make the final chapter feel inevitable rather than isolated.

label: How To Use The Timeline
notes: Make the timeline operational. When a theorem feels isolated, locate its lane, ask which invariant it preserves, and identify which earlier computational check would test the same idea. This turns review into an active diagnostic routine instead of rereading headings.

label: Takeaways
notes: Close with the course arc. The timeline gives learners a way to revisit the notebooks as a connected atlas rather than a sequence of separate chapters. The final prompt is practical: choose a lane, name an invariant, then find the computation that verifies it.
